Waco

Waco names a historical people whose individual identity remains visible within Wichita-affiliated history. Carolyn Garrett Pool’s focused account and the Wichita and Affiliated Tribes’ own connected narrative provide a starting path. This route does not create a separate present-day Waco government or treat every affiliated people as another name for the same community.

Read the sources [1] Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture [2] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey

01

Texas places and removal

Pool places Waco communities among the Wichita on Red River and with Tawakoni communities on the Sabine in the mid-eighteenth century. Her article then follows assignment to the Brazos Indian Reservation near Fort Belknap in 1855 and removal to Indian Territory in 1859. These are the author’s historical synthesis and chronology; treaty implementation and every family’s experience require other records. The modern Brazos-at-Waco photograph is local river context, not a surviving Waco village.

Read the sources [1] Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture [3] City of Waco

02

Affiliation and continuing identity

The article emphasizes separate Waco villages and recognized headmen during the reservation era, even while Waco people were administratively grouped with the Wichita. Its discussion of allotment and late-twentieth-century family identification shows why a shared political framework should not erase historical names. Read that scholarly account alongside the Tribe’s own history, which explicitly includes Waco among its named peoples. Neither source establishes an individual reader’s descent or current citizenship.

Read the sources [1] Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture [2] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey

Scholarly referenceOklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and CultureSource 1

Waco ↗

Publication: 2010-01-15

Carolyn Garrett Pool’s focused article distinguishes Waco historical identity from the wider Wichita and Affiliated Tribes. It follows Texas locations, the Brazos reservation, removal and reservation-era villages. Its end-of-twentieth-century statement remains dated; no separate current Waco government or individual descent is established.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete main body, web lines 98–102, byline, bibliography and January 15, 2010 publication metadata read. Bibliography and original records were not separately opened; opening federal-recognition wording is not independently audited or converted into a separate Waco-government claim.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access note: Actual public HTML body readable without an account in this inspection. Linked bibliography, archival instruments and media remain separate works unless expressly listed.

Wichita Memories — four connected institutional history chapters ↗

Four linked chapters explain the Tribe’s historical account from early encounters through village life, displacement and continuing community. The credits identify a cooperative exhibit. Treat the chapters as one work, keep named historical groups distinct, and attribute archaeological, treaty and continuity interpretations rather than turning the narrative into independently checked archival evidence.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete main narratives of In the Beginning:1540–1750 (lines27–38), People of the Grass House:1750–1820 (27–39), Days of Darkness:1820–1934 (27–37), and A New Beginning:1934–Present (27–38), plus References and Contributors (27–91). Public narrative passages read; no quoted origin stories, ceremonial details, images or underlying bibliography reproduced or separately researched.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access note: Public readable English HTML, no account/paywall encountered. Individual publication/revision dates are unstated; date ranges in titles are historical coverage, not publication dates. Do not repeat historical population estimates as current figures, infer present identities from archaeological phases, or treat institutional treaty summaries as direct readings of the instruments.

A History of Indian Spring Park — selected public-place context ↗

Publication: Updated 2025-01-02

Municipal public-history context for a modern Brazos-at-Waco image. The page locates Indian Spring Park on the Brazos and describes a 1911 commemoration of Waco campgrounds. This demonstrates the city’s place interpretation, not a surveyed Indigenous village boundary, community endorsement or proof that all photographed riverbank was Waco-owned.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Scope: Actual selected main-body paragraphs at web lines 29 and 35–36, with January 2, 2025 update metadata read. Other visitor, sculpture and event material encountered but not adopted. Underlying city/Baylor/DAR records and images not inspected or reproduced.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026
